title: The history of the transformer
tagline: Nearly two centuries from Faraday's iron ring to the 1,200 kV giants tested in Madhya Pradesh.
intro: In 1831 Michael Faraday wound two coils on an iron ring and found that switching one on made a current flicker in the other. Fifty years later inventors in London, Budapest and Massachusetts turned that trick into a machine that could change AC voltage at will, and alternating current won the race to power the world. Since then transformers have grown to hundreds of megavolt-amperes, their cores have become thinner and cleverer, and India has built its own, from Bhopal to the 1,200 kV test station at Bina.

eras.name: Discovering induction
eras.summary: Electricity makes magnetism, and changing magnetism makes electricity. Two coils on one ring become the first transformer, though no one calls it that yet.

eras.name: The transformer is born
eras.summary: Gaulard and Gibbs, then the Ganz engineers in Budapest and William Stanley in America, build practical transformers that let one AC line feed many lamps at a safe voltage.

eras.name: AC wins and spreads
eras.summary: The war of the currents ends in AC's favour. Three-phase lines run for hundreds of kilometres, and India builds some of the earliest long high-voltage lines.

eras.name: Better steel, oil and protection
eras.summary: Oil cooling, silicon steel, grain-oriented steel, the Buchholz relay and glassy amorphous metal make transformers cooler, safer and far less wasteful.

eras.name: India builds its own
eras.summary: BHEL starts making heavy electrical equipment in Bhopal, then transformers in Jhansi, and India's grid grows into one national network.

eras.name: Extra and ultra-high voltage
eras.summary: Line voltages climb from 287 kV to 1,150 kV. India runs 765 kV lines, tests 1,200 kV, and tightens the efficiency rules for its street transformers.

events.title: A current moves a compass needle
events.text: During a lecture, Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying current made a nearby compass needle swing. He published the result in July 1820. It was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked.
events.why: If a current makes magnetism, people began to ask whether magnetism could make a current.

events.title: Faraday's induction ring
events.text: Faraday wound two separate coils of wire on an iron ring. When he connected a battery to one coil, a needle connected to the other coil flicked, then fell back. It flicked again, the other way, when he disconnected. A current appeared only while the magnetism was changing.
events.why: This ring was, in effect, the first transformer: two coils sharing one iron core.

events.title: Henry finds induction too
events.text: Working separately, the American Joseph Henry also found that a changing current in one coil induces a current in another, and he discovered self-induction. Faraday published first, so the law carries his name.
events.why: Two independent discoveries showed induction was a real, repeatable effect of nature.

events.title: The induction coil
events.text: Callan wound a short primary of thick wire and a long secondary of thin wire on an iron core, and broke the primary current rapidly. The secondary gave sparks of very high voltage. Induction coils like his were used for decades in labs, and later for X-rays and car ignition.
events.why: It showed that more turns on the secondary means a higher voltage: stepping up.

events.title: Gaulard and Gibbs's secondary generator
events.who: Lucien Gaulard and John Dixon Gibbs
events.text: The Frenchman Gaulard and the Englishman Gibbs showed a device they called a secondary generator: coils on an open iron core that lowered an AC voltage for lamps. Their coils were connected in series along the line, which made each lamp affect the others.
events.why: It was the first system to use induction coils to distribute electricity at a different voltage from the line.

events.title: A 34 km test line in Turin
events.text: For the International Exhibition of Electricity in Turin, Gaulard's system ran a line about 34 km long, fed by a 2,000 V, 130 Hz Siemens & Halske alternator. It worked well and was taken up for electric lighting.
events.why: It proved AC with transformers could carry power over tens of kilometres.

events.title: A closed core, and the word “transformer”
events.who: Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri
events.text: Three engineers at the Ganz works built transformers with a closed iron core, so almost all the flux linked both coils, and connected them in parallel across the line. They filed their patents between January and March 1885. Bláthy is credited with coining the name “transformer”.
events.why: Closed cores and parallel connection are how every power transformer has worked since.

events.title: 75 transformers light an exhibition
events.text: At the Hungarian National Exhibition, a 1,350 V AC generator fed 75 ZBD transformers connected in parallel. Together they lit 1,067 lamps of 60 V.
events.why: It was the first public show of a practical transformer distribution system.

events.title: Great Barrington lights up
events.who: William Stanley Jr., for George Westinghouse
events.text: Stanley stepped a 500 V generator's output up to 3,000 V, sent it along wires strung on the elm trees of Main Street, and stepped it down again. Transformers in the basements of shops and offices fed their lamps at about 100 V.
events.why: It was the first complete AC system in the USA with step-up and step-down transformers, now an IEEE Milestone.

events.title: The war of the currents
events.who: Thomas Edison against George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla
events.text: Edison's companies sold low-voltage DC, which could only reach a kilometre or two from a power station. Westinghouse sold AC, which transformers could step up for long lines. Westinghouse bought Tesla's AC motor patents in 1888, and after a bitter public fight his company won the contract to light the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
events.why: The transformer was AC's winning card: DC had no simple way to change voltage.

events.title: Three-phase power crosses 175 km
events.who: Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky, AEG and Oskar von Miller
events.where: Lauffen am Neckar to Frankfurt, Germany
events.text: Dolivo-Dobrovolsky developed three-phase generators, motors and transformers at AEG. In 1891 a 15 kV three-phase line about 175 km long carried power from a hydro plant at Lauffen to the electrical exhibition in Frankfurt.
events.why: It showed that three-phase AC, with transformers at each end, could move power across a country.

events.title: Transformers go into oil
events.text: Early transformers were cooled by air and insulated with cloth and shellac. In a patent filed on 28 August 1891, Elihu Thomson of the Thomson-Houston company described transformers that could be enclosed in oil. Oil-filled tanks soon became the usual design for larger units.
events.why: Oil insulates far better than air and carries heat away, so transformers could be made bigger and more compact at once.

events.title: Niagara powers Buffalo
events.who: Westinghouse and the Niagara Falls Power Company
events.where: Niagara Falls to Buffalo, New York, USA
events.text: AC from the new hydroelectric plant at Niagara Falls was stepped up and sent about 40 km to the city of Buffalo. More lines and more customers followed.
events.why: It confirmed AC and transformers as the way to build large power systems.

events.title: India's first hydro station
events.text: The Sidrapong hydel station near Darjeeling began with two 65 kW generators to light the hill town. It was later expanded to about 1,000 kW and still stands.
events.why: It began India's story of generating and distributing electricity.

events.title: Silicon steel
events.text: Hadfield had made iron alloyed with silicon in the 1880s. Around 1900, he and the physicist William Barrett reported that it has much lower magnetic losses than plain iron. Silicon steel soon replaced iron in transformer cores.
events.why: Silicon raises the steel's resistance, weakening eddy currents, so cores wasted much less energy.

events.title: Sivasamudram to the Kolar Gold Fields
events.who: Mysore State: Dewan K. Seshadri Iyer and engineer A. C. Joly de Lotbinière
events.where: Shivanasamudra Falls to Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka, India
events.text: A hydro plant at the Kaveri falls sent power about 147 km to the gold mines at Kolar. Transformers raised the voltage to around 30,000–35,000 V for the journey and lowered it again at the mines. It was among the longest high-voltage lines in the world at the time.
events.why: It was India's first long-distance high-voltage line, and it later brought electric light to Bengaluru.

events.title: Hydropower for Bombay's mills
events.text: Tata's hydro station at Khopoli in the Western Ghats started sending power over high-voltage lines to Bombay's textile mills.
events.why: It showed Indian industry could run on power made far away and carried by transformers and lines.

events.title: The Buchholz relay
events.text: Buchholz, a senior official at the Prussian electricity company, studied damaged transformers and saw that internal arcs break the oil down into gas. He designed a relay for the pipe to the conservator that collects that gas to raise an alarm, and trips the transformer on a sudden surge of oil.
events.why: It gave oil-filled transformers an early warning of faults inside, and it is still fitted today.

events.title: Grain-oriented steel
events.text: Goss patented a way of rolling and annealing silicon steel so its crystals line up along the sheet. Flux flows far more easily in that direction. This cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) steel became the standard for power transformer cores.
events.why: CRGO cut core losses sharply, and almost every large transformer core still uses it.

events.title: 287 kV from Hoover Dam
events.who: Los Angeles Bureau of Power and Light
events.where: Hoover (Boulder) Dam to Los Angeles, USA
events.text: A 287.5 kV line about 428 km (266 miles) long began carrying power from Hoover Dam to Los Angeles, the highest transmission voltage of its day.
events.why: Higher voltage let distant dams feed growing cities.

events.title: The first 380 kV line
events.text: Sweden opened the world's first 380 kV AC line, running about 1,000 km from hydro plants in the far north towards the south.
events.why: 380–400 kV became the backbone voltage of grids across Europe and, later, India.

events.title: Heavy electricals in Bhopal
events.text: India set up Heavy Electricals (India) Limited on 29 August 1956, with help from Associated Electrical Industries of Britain. Its Bhopal factory, which makes transformers among other equipment, was dedicated to the nation in November 1960. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited was formed in 1964.
events.why: India began making its own power transformers instead of importing them.

events.title: 735 kV in Québec
events.text: Hydro-Québec switched on the world's first 735 kV line, bringing hydropower about 600 km south to Montréal.
events.why: It opened the era of extra-high-voltage transmission, now an IEEE Milestone.

events.title: A transformer factory in Jhansi
events.text: BHEL set up a dedicated transformer plant at Jhansi as part of its second wave of factories, making power and traction transformers for India's growing grid and railways.
events.why: Transformer making in India grew to match the grid's rapid expansion.

events.title: Amorphous metal cores
events.who: Allied Corporation (Metglas), EPRI and US utilities
events.text: Metals cooled so fast that they freeze without crystals can be magnetised with very little loss. Ribbons of this amorphous metal, about 0.025 mm thick, were made into transformer cores from the late 1970s, and US utilities installed hundreds of thousands of amorphous-core distribution transformers.
events.why: They cut no-load losses by around 70 per cent, and India now uses them too.

events.title: The 1,150 kV record
events.text: A 432 km line in Kazakhstan was commissioned at 1,150 kV, still the highest AC voltage ever used in regular service. After 1991 it was run at 500 kV.
events.why: It showed the limits of AC transmission, and the huge transformers such lines need.

events.title: India's first 765 kV line
events.where: Sipat, Chhattisgarh, to Seoni, Madhya Pradesh, India
events.text: POWERGRID's 351 km Sipat–Seoni line and its 765/400 kV substation at Seoni brought 765 kV transmission to India. 765 kV corridors now link coal, hydro and solar regions to distant cities.
events.why: One 765 kV line carries as much power as several 400 kV lines on less land.

events.title: A 1,200 kV transformer at Bina
events.text: A 333 MVA, 1,150/400/33 kV single-phase transformer designed and built by BHEL in Bhopal energised the 1,200 kV National Test Station at Bina, set up by POWERGRID with Indian manufacturers. A second phase was charged in 2016.
events.why: India joined the few countries able to build ultra-high-voltage AC equipment.

events.title: One Nation, One Grid
events.where: Raichur, Karnataka, to Solapur, Maharashtra, India
events.text: The 765 kV Raichur–Solapur line synchronised the southern grid with the rest of India, making one national grid running at one frequency.
events.why: Power can now flow from any region to any other, through transformers at every step.

events.title: Tougher star labels for transformers
events.text: BEE's revised star labelling for distribution transformers took effect, extending the scheme to 11 kV units up to 2,500 kVA and lowering the allowed losses: the old 4 and 5 stars became the new 1 and 2. The limits line up with the energy-efficiency levels of the BIS standard IS 1180.
events.why: With millions of transformers humming day and night, small cuts in loss save a great deal of energy.

people.note: Discovered electromagnetic induction with two coils on an iron ring.

people.note: With Gibbs, built the first transformer system for distributing AC lighting.

people.note: Gaulard's partner, who backed and co-patented the secondary generator.

people.note: Co-inventor of the closed-core ZBD transformer, credited with naming it.

people.name: Miksa Déri

people.name: William Stanley Jr.
people.note: Built Westinghouse's first practical transformers and the Great Barrington system.

facts: The name “transformer” comes from the Ganz engineers in Budapest in 1885; Ottó Bláthy is usually credited with it.
Transformers hum at 100 Hz in India, twice the mains frequency: the core's steel stretches very slightly on every half-cycle, whichever way the flux points.
Eddy-current loss grows with the square of the lamination thickness, which is why core sheets are only about a quarter of a millimetre thick.
Paper insulation ages about twice as fast for every 6 °C above 98 °C, so a transformer's life depends on how hot its hottest spot gets.
On 30 and 31 July 2012, grid failures in north and east India left more than 600 million people without power.
